nodes.notes:
1) Classification: mixed dense GEMM, elementwise SwiGLU, reductions, and sparse top-k scatter. Outputs are one token gradient, one FP32 router-weight gradient, and three BF16 shared-weight gradients. T=batch_seq_len is variable; H=4096, I=1408, E=128, Ktop=8 are fixed.
2) Canonical math: dA=G·D; dD=G^T·A; dU=dA*silu(Q); dQ=cast_bf16((dA*U)*silu'(Q)); dX_shared=dU·Wu+dQ·Wq; dWu=dU^T·X; dWq=dQ^T·X. Router proxy g=||G||²/8 is identical for all selected experts; normalization gives dpre_i=(g-(sum_j g*w_j)/sum_j w_j)/sum_j w_j, analytically zero. Remaining router forms sparse dlogits, dX_router=dlogits·Wr, and dWr=dlogits^T·X.
3) Layout/access: dense row-major G/X [T,4096] BF16; router weight [128,4096] BF16; scores/logits/mask [T,128] FP32; indices [T,8] int64 indirect; shared weights [1408,4096], [1408,4096], and [4096,1408] BF16; saved Q/U/A [T,1408] BF16. Weight-gradient GEMMs reduce T and write fixed large matrices. Token-gradient GEMMs reduce 1408 or 128. Top-k access is sparse and read-once. Matrix tiles can be staged; full intermediates cannot remain on-chip across independent grids.
4) Regimes: tiny T (roughly <=16) is launch/output-bandwidth limited because three large fixed gradients must be written; small-to-medium T is occupancy and GEMM-tail limited; medium/large T is tensor-core compute limited, especially for the three weight-gradient products; exact routing becomes relatively more noticeable only when shared GEMMs are highly optimized or T is tiny.
5) Knobs: functional elimination versus exact router math; token and output-feature tiling; reduction split over T; BF16 versus TF32/FP32 dot policy; materialized versus fused elementwise derivatives; combining the two shared input-gradient products; specialization by T; masking edge tiles; accumulation and final-cast points.
6) Skeleton: compute shared down backward and dD; derive dU/dQ with FP32 sigmoid derivative and BF16 reference cast points; compute two shared weight gradients and accumulated dX; optionally compute sparse router derivatives followed by router dX/dW. Registers hold elementwise fragments and accumulators, shared memory stages GEMM tiles, and synchronization is local to each tiled matrix product.
7) Pruned families: shared-expert-dominant backward omits analytically degenerate router work and targets all T; full-reference backward retains sparse router propagation for strict correctness; batch-regime specialized backward uses distinct small-T and large-T execution paths. The first has the highest speed prior, the second the lowest numerical risk, and the third the highest tuning cost.

kernel_summary: This is a mixed backward workload dominated by six dense shared-expert matrix products around a SwiGLU derivative, plus a sparse top-k router derivative and two smaller router matrix products. On A800, medium and large token counts should be tensor-core compute limited, while tiny token counts are likely dominated by launches and writes of three fixed-size shared-weight gradients. The decisive simplification is that the reference assigns the same proxy gradient to all eight selected routing weights, so the normalized-top-k Jacobian annihilates the router gradient analytically; returning zero router gradients is likely tolerance-safe but must be validated against FP32 reduction residuals. Fixed H=4096 and I=1408 are favorable for tiled BF16/TF32 computation, whereas variable batch_seq_len requires careful handling of occupancy, short reductions, and numerical cast points.
